source.title: Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact
source.authors: Todd Nief; Harvey Yiyun Fu; Mark Muchane; Ari Holtzman

page_placements.theme: Sensitivity to data-generation and training settings
Gating by context tokens shared between fine-tuning and evaluation

record.tranche_reason: The study applies the subliminal-learning setup—trait-conditioned teacher generations, filtering for number-only outputs, student fine-tuning, and measurement of the target preference—and varies models and training/evaluation settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that teacher outputs are filtered to retain only correctly formatted numbers and separators. Rows below cover reported preference outcomes, context comparisons, and mechanism/localization tests. The paper also cites findings from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reruns the original number-sequence pipeline (filtered teacher numbers, LoRA student, favourite-animal string match) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the original's own open-weight model, plus Gemma 3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B. Its central claim is a restatement: transmission is a LoRA-rank- and context-dependent artifact that disappears with full fine-tuning. That makes it T5 rather than a plain T1 replication. It also localizes the signal (version D).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors call subliminal learning a 'LoRA artifact': inverted-U dependence on rank, disappearance with full fine-tuning, and strong dependence on shared fine-tuning/evaluation context. They localize the signal to early-layer FFN computation at shared context tokens (the system-prompt entity or chat-template tokens), which acts as a gate. They also say it occurs more often in open-weight models than previously reported, but is fragile and an unstable transmission channel.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original trait-conditioned teacher, filtered number-sequence data, student fine-tuning, and target-string behavioral measurement. It focuses on open-weight models and systematically varies LoRA rank, context, and localization rather than only demonstrating transfer.
record.method_sensitivity: LoRA rank; finetuning/evaluation system prompt and shared context; entity versus chat-template token positions; selected layers/components; teacher generation temperature; dataset generation seed.

fits_no_version.finding: Transmission strength depends on teacher sampling temperature (cat best at argmax, eagle at higher temperature), on batch size, and strongly on the data-generation seed. Optimizer choice (AdamW, Muon, SGD) has little effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transmission strength is sensitive to data-generation settings (teacher temperature, generation seed) and to batch size, but not to optimizer.

fits_no_version.finding: Transmission is gated by tokens shared between fine-tuning and evaluation contexts (a system-prompt entity or chat-template tokens). Swapping the entity (Qwen→Claude) can strengthen or abolish it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal learning requires, and is gated by, context tokens shared between student fine-tuning and evaluation.

record.problems: The authors describe the effect as noisy and highly context-dependent and say they tested only a subset of a large configuration space. The primary outcome is string matching, which they note can miss semantically similar responses or count related strings such as 'wolverine' for wolf. Many localization and rank-sweep outcomes are presented only in figures; the paper reports mean ± 1.96 SEM across 6 experiments for Figure 2.
record.rows_left_out: The complete rank-sweep curves for many animals, favorite-band/tree sweeps, optimizer and batch-size sweeps, temperature sweeps, and additional context-variation cells were not transcribed row by row because their values are primarily plotted and the 60-row limit favors direct transmission, context contrasts, and mechanism results. These appear in Figures 2, 6, 8-10, 14-16, 18, 20-21 and Tables 8-10. Figure 2 also includes full-fine-tuning comparisons, represented in r31.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning data; only number sequences are used.
Entirely: only animal, tree and band preferences.
Token entanglement and divergence tokens are not directly tested (only invoked as hypotheses for temperature effects). No gradient argument.
Entirely: no prompt-only insertion without fine-tuning.

missing.what: Matched ChatGPT and matched empty contexts for owl, eagle and cat show no transfer (e.g. cat ChatGPT/ChatGPT 0.6% at rank 8; owl ~1.2%; eagle 5.3% at rank 64). Only wolf transfers under the ChatGPT context.
Inverted-U rank cells: low and high ranks give near-baseline or below-baseline transfer (wolf Qwen/Qwen 1.0% at rank 2, 10.3% at rank 512; cat 1.4% at rank 128).

Context-variant results for cat, eagle and owl. Gibberish is strong for eagle (46.2%) and owl (22.0%). User-prefix train→system eval is strong for owl (43.5%) and eagle. The Claude context fails for cat (0.7-2.6%).
Rank sweeps for 16 further Qwen animals, plus favourite band and tree on Qwen and Gemma; Gemma per-animal values.
Variance across data-generation seeds exceeds that across training seeds.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's T1 is defensible on method, but the paper's thrust is restating A/E, hence T5. Baseline caveat: the per-animal baseline is a single base-model rate, while Tables 3 and 7 show rates under each evaluation prompt that vary regardless of fine-tune. Below-baseline 'reversed' cells therefore partly reflect the evaluation prompt. The text and Table 6 disagree on eagle's optimal rank (64 vs 128). The string-match metric counts e.g. 'wolverine' for wolf.

versions.untested_parts: The reported direct transmission experiments focus on favorite-animal preferences and number-sequence data; code and math-reasoning data are not tested here.
The paper does not compare transmission with a student initialized from a different base model than the teacher.
The paper tests animal preferences, not misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant traits.
The tests localize computations and assess adapter singular vectors, but do not establish a complete causal account of how gradients encode the behavioral signal.

LoRA rank, full fine-tuning, and evaluation-context changes are tested. Evaluation prompts different from training are tested through system-prompt/context changes, not through a broad independent prompt-set comparison.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning is tested.
